title: In and out
hook: some things hurry into being, others out, and the whole is a river (Meditations 6.15)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stepmother and the mother, the duty and the home you keep returning to. Your line was visit the mother.

Stand in a hospital for one hour and you'd see it from both ends. On one floor, someone is born. On another, someone's family is saying goodbye. In the lobby, a man is buying flowers, and the flowers, already cut, have started to fade. Most days we only see one end at a time, so the whole thing stays invisible. Marcus Aurelius, in book six, tries to see both ends at once.
screen: `A HOSPITAL, BOTH ENDS.` → `FLOWERS ALREADY FADING.` → `ARRIVING AND LEAVING AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Meditations six, fifteen, in George Long's translation, begins: "Some things are hurrying into existence, and others are hurrying out of it." Not drifting. Hurrying. The world is a doorway with traffic both ways. Then the twist: of what is coming into being, part is already gone. The new day starts ending at dawn. A song is partly over by its second verse. Arrival and departure aren't two events. They're one motion seen from two sides. Then he asks: in a stream like this, where nothing stays, what passing thing would you set a high price on? It would be like falling in love with one of the sparrows flying past, and it's already out of sight. That can sound bleak. But read it slowly. He isn't saying don't love. He's saying don't stake your peace on holding any one sparrow still. Seeing both ends at once is oddly steadying. When something you love arrives, you can greet it knowing it's passing, and so pay closer attention. When something you dread arrives, you know it's also already on its way out. Marcus doesn't ask you to stop caring. He asks you to care with your eyes open, the way you'd watch a sparrow: fully, and without trying to close your hand.
screen: `HURRYING IN, HURRYING OUT.` · `PART OF EVERY ARRIVAL IS GONE.` · `IN LOVE WITH A PASSING SPARROW.` · `CARE WITH YOUR EYES OPEN.` · then, large: `IN AND OUT.`

segments.voice: Each breath is a tiny version of Marcus's sentence: air hurrying in, air hurrying out. Watch one breath begin and end. Then find one thing around you that's beginning, a sound, a thought, and one that's ending, and hold both lightly, without grabbing either.
Marcus, who pictured the world as a doorway with traffic both ways, where even what arrives is already leaving. Today's word.
Your line: already out of sight. Care fully, without closing your hand. That's day five hundred seventy-seven.

screen: `DAY 577 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SCRATCH IN THE GYM.`

howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus practice noticing beginnings and endings during the day, as a way to hold things they care about with attention rather than a tight grip.

fork.setup: something you love has just arrived: a visit, a season, a good stretch. by Marcus's picture, how do you hold it?
options: grip it hard so it can't leave.
refuse to enjoy it, since it will end.
enjoy it fully, knowing it's already passing.
fork.reveal: Meditations 6.15 sees arrival and departure as one motion; the sparrow is loved by watching, not by grabbing.

what a scholar hears: 6.15 sits in a run of entries on flux; Marcus's image of time as a river echoes Heraclitus, whom he names elsewhere in the Meditations.

chat.says: If everything passes so fast, why let yourself love anything at all?

Hold on tighter, so the things you love can't slip away.

chat.meaning: Marcus says prizing a passing thing is like loving a sparrow flying by. Don't stop caring; care with your eyes open, without clutching.
